item.title: Organ-scale pulsatile blood flow reconstruction in the avian yolk sac embryo
item.description: arXiv:2611.28228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hemodynamic forces on endothelial cells in developing vascular networks vary over the cardiac cycle. Resolving these variations throughout the yolk sac requires imaging individual regions of the vasculature at different times. We reconstructed mean and pulsatile blood flow in a 21-somite quail embryo from 53 overlapping high-speed microscopy recordings acquired over 3.7 h. We reconciled mean-flow measurements using conservation of flux at vascular junctions and synchronized cardiac phases using vessels shared between recordings. Of the 7,009 vessels with flow measurements in the computational domain, we reconstructed pulsatile flow in 5,214. Relative pulsatility decreased along an arterial-side path but increased along a venous-return path, where downstream flow oscillations preceded those upstream. Across the plexus, phase lags relative to the vitelline veins increased toward the vascular margin. A distributed resistance--compliance model with uniform vessel distensibility reproduced many of these spatial variations. Our results suggest that vascular geometry and compliance, together with pulsatile forcing from both arterial and venous boundaries, determine the local flow waveforms within the developing plexus.
item.dc:creator: Sidney Holden, Alexander Mayer, Siavash Ghaffari, Elizabeth A. V. Jones, Eleni Katifori

item.title: Dynamics of the Nuclear Envelope and Mitotic Spindle in Closed Mitosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.28302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: During closed mitosis, large-scale deformation of the nuclear envelope is driven by the mitotic spindle and chromosomes contained within it. Previous models of closed mitosis have established that the spatial distribution of spindle-generated forces influences nuclear morphology, but have imposed axisymmetry and focused on equilibrium shapes. We introduce a three-dimensional biophysical model of nuclear envelope remodeling and spindle elongation that incorporates thermal fluctuations to examine how spindle-generated forces, chromatin distribution, and nuclear envelope elasticity control nuclear shape in fission yeast. The model reproduces features of both successful and aberrant nuclear shape change, including centering of mispositioned spindles, the dumbbell nuclear shape transition, and the formation of nuclear protrusions. A phase diagram of nuclear shape shows that insufficient spindle force produces elongated but undivided nuclei, while sufficiently large spindle forces produce either symmetric division or envelope tethers, depending on the size of the chromatin-envelope contact region. Near the boundary between symmetric division and tethering, nuclei develop asymmetric single-tether configurations. A reduced-order representation of the coupled envelope-spindle system shows a symmetry-breaking transition between symmetric and asymmetric nuclear shapes. Below a critical chromatin-envelope contact size, symmetric configurations lose stability during spindle elongation and thermal fluctuations drive nuclear shape trajectories toward one of two stable asymmetric configurations. These findings identify a growth-driven mechanical mechanism for spindle centering and alignment during early mitosis and reveal how asymmetric nuclear morphologies can arise during anaphase even in the absence of structural differences between the two spindle poles.
item.dc:creator: Wilson Lough, Zachary R. Gergely, Eduardo Corona, Meredith D. Betterton

item.title: Estimating Extrapolation Factors in Time-Resolved Crystallography
item.description: arXiv:2611.28961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved crystallography (TRX) captures macromolecules in action, but a triggered crystal contains a mixture of triggered proteins in an unknown state and untriggered proteins in the reference state. Separating these is necessary to isolate the dynamics of interest and is an underdetermined data-analysis task. For the simplest case, with one triggered state and one reference state, a range of methods exists, but their assumptions, accuracy, and domains of applicability have not been systematically investigated. Here, we deconstruct and review the methods in current use, employing a unified notation. We make their assumptions explicit and benchmark each on a simulated dataset. A key point is that many of these methods do not estimate the fraction of all triggered molecules in the crystal, but instead estimate a latent parameter we call the extrapolation factor, which is related to but distinct from the so-called "occupancy". As our simulations make apparent, current methods do not always yield accurate results, in particular with noisy data and when the fraction of triggered protein is low. Inspired by previous work, we introduce Vacuum Level Matching, a method that grounds the estimate in the physical constraint that electron density is a nonnegative quantity: it cannot fall below a vacuum level. Operating voxel by voxel, Vacuum Level Matching replaces the manual choices of previous methods with a data-driven procedure and reports quality-control metrics that flag data unable to support a confident prediction. On the same simulated data, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and on two experimental datasets, rsEGFP2 and a multi-time-point photolyase series, it recovers known structural changes while flagging issues where the data are weak. Finally, we report an implementation of Vacuum Level Matching in the form of a small, reusable Python package.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Bielfeldt, Henry N. Chapman, Thomas J. Lane

item.title: Infrared Relaxation Modes and the Emergence of Collective Order in Neural Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.29880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a microscopic field theory of collective order formation in interacting nonlinear neural systems. Integrating out microscopic neural degrees of freedom yields an effective action whose quadratic kernel determines the ordering threshold, while higher-order connected responses govern nonlinear stabilization. Spectral decomposition reveals that relaxation rates and collective-mode overlaps control collective instability and memory dynamics. Enhanced infrared spectral weight lowers the critical coupling and generates long-time memory, revealing a common spectral origin of collective ordering and persistent dynamics. Controlled numerical constructions verify the spectral dependence of collective instability and response, while nonlinear mean-field scaling follows from the microscopic Landau expansion. Transformer Jacobian spectra further reveal learning-induced infrared organization and transient memory enhancement consistent with critical-like response. Our results establish a microscopic framework linking neural interactions, collective order, and long-time memory.
item.dc:creator: Byung Gyu Chae

item.title: Impact of Topology and Sequence Length on the Pressure-Dependent Collapsibility of Proteins
item.description: arXiv:2611.30336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several physical and evolutionary factors, including temperature, pressure, solvent quality, and natural selection, influence how amino acid sequences adopt their native structures. Although protein folding has been extensively studied, the physical determinants of protein collapse and their relationship to native-state folding remain less understood. In particular, "collapsibility", the intrinsic propensity of a protein sequence to form compact conformations, is distinct from but closely related to "foldability", the ability to reach the native structure. Previous theoretical studies suggested that collapsibility is encoded in native-state topology, potentially reflecting evolutionary selection. However, the roles of solvent-mediated interactions and hydrostatic pressure remain unclear. Here, we extend the theoretical framework of protein collapsibility by incorporating a pressure-dependent desolvation potential to investigate how hydrostatic pressure influences protein collapse. We find that increasing pressure destabilizes the fully folded native state, but can still favor the compact, water-mediated conformations. Furthermore, the magnitude and direction of pressure-induced changes in collapsibility depend strongly on native-state topology, including secondary and tertiary structures. Proteins and domains with a higher proportion of non-local native contacts generally exhibit greater pressure-induced water-mediated collapsibility. These findings highlight the role of native-state topology in determining the pressure sensitivity of protein collapse and provide insights into the interplay among protein structure, solvent-mediated interactions, and environmental perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Jiayi Wang, D. Thirumalai, Margaret S. Cheung, Andrei G. Gasic

item.title: Nonequilibrium fluctuations could explain the hot mitochondria paradox
item.description: arXiv:2611.28225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Several different experiments have found apparent temperature differences of up to 10 K between the interior of mitochondria and the rest of the cellular environment. The physics of heat conduction, however, precludes the steady-state existence of a temperature difference greater than the microkelvin scale within the cell, absent a far greater energy budget. Nearly a decade after the first reported measurement, this apparent paradox remains unexplained. Here, we propose an explanation which allows the elevated temperature measurements to coexist with the theoretical impossibility of a true 10 K steady-state temperature difference. We suggest that nonequilibrium fluctuations within the cellular environment, combined with molecular temperature probes sensitive to specific ranges of frequencies, can lead to apparent 10 K temperature differences with a biologically attainable power budget.
item.dc:creator: Matthew P. Leighton, Benjamin B. Machta

item.title: Dynamic Renewal for Hydrodynamic Coupling in Ciliary Mucus Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.29378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mucociliary clearance in large mammalian airways involves millimetric MUC5B-rich mucus strands that emerge from submucosal glands approximately aligned with the direction of transport. These strands are observed downstream in cross-flow networks. Recently, Bos et al. [PNAS Nexus 2, pgad388 (2023)] modeled single strand reorientation using a free-draining coupling for the flow induced by cilia. This leaves unresolved whether the strand's own disturbance of the surrounding liquid assists or frustrates the turning. Here, we develop the methodology to address this question. An immersed-boundary coupling is combined with a Fourier-space Stokes solver and a bespoke dynamic-renewal algorithm that exposes the strand to new ciliary domain without enlarging the simulation volume. This allows us to overcome one of the multiscale challenges posed by mucociliary clearance. We find that hydrodynamic interactions result in only a limited decrease in the rate of reorientation, which supports the use of the free-draining approximation. Future work can build on the methodological foundation introduced here to study collective strand dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jeroen Bechtold, Valentijn van Zwieten, Iris Verkuil, Meike F. Bos, Georg Rempfer, Mae Nesenberend, Pieter Michels, Florian K. R. Gaeremynck, Bart Stam, Debabrata Panja, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Exact superdiffusion exponents and hull exploration of chiral random walkers on critical percolation clusters
item.description: arXiv:2611.29537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalizing de Gennes' ant-in-the-labyrinth concept, we consider a chiral random walker on a percolation cluster at criticality. The fully chiral ant clings to obstacle boundaries and traces the fractal hulls of the cluster, spreading with the exact walk dimension $7/4$ until its orbit closes. Because the cluster contains holes on all scales, the ensemble spreads superdiffusively, $\langle r^2\rangle\sim t^{89/84}$, carried by a diminishing fraction of walkers whose orbits are still open. Both exponents follow from percolation geometry alone, and agree well with large-scale numerical simulations. When the walker turns chirally only with probability $\chi<1$, superdiffusion gives way to the subdiffusion of the ant at a crossover time set by both exponents, with a diffusion coefficient enhanced by $(1-\chi)^{-2/d_w}$. The relation between crossover time and diffusion coefficient does not depend on how chirality is realized, offering a direct test for chiral tracers in disordered media.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Uhlig, Ralf Metzler, Erik Kalz

item.title: Growing Knot Embeddings into Spherical Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30245v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knotted structures occur throughout soft matter and biology, where topological constraints can shape relaxation and spatial organization. Here, we introduce a computational construction that maps a specific 3D knot embedding to a graph embedded on the sphere through growth and interfacial-energy relaxation. For standard 3D embeddings of prime knots with at most seven crossings, we obtain a family of growth-based graphs that generally differ from the corresponding Tait graphs. We further identify an empirical growth-graph reconstruction rule based on polygonal regions with alternating crossing structure in a knot diagram. Non-minimal diagrams demonstrate that these graphs are not knot invariants, while selected connected sums suggest that graph features associated with their prime factors can remain recognizable. Determining how these graphs transform under isotopy may reveal invariant features, which we leave for future study.
item.dc:creator: Eren G\"ulmez, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish
item.description: arXiv:2611.31170v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fluid flows enable and limit the feeding and locomotion of sea creatures across a wide range of scales. Although much is known about how microorganisms navigate life at low Reynolds numbers, the effect of inertial flows on the feeding-efficiency of larger marine organisms remains less well understood. Here, using jellyfish as an archetypal example, we study the trade-off between prey capture rate and energy expended to generate inertial flows by surface deformations. We develop a feeding-efficiency landscape that predicts an optimal feeding regime at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, mediated by a self-generated vortex ring. These predictions provide a unifying biophysical explanation of size and beat frequencies reported for jellyfish species from different taxa, with vortex-ring-dominated transport supported by our experimental observations for the moon jellyfish \textit{Aurelia aurita}. More broadly, our results demonstrate how centimetric marine predators can exploit inertial flows for efficient prey capture.
item.dc:creator: Harry Walden, Ashutosh Tripathi, Teo Lara, Brandon Weissbourd, J\"orn Dunkel

item.title: Self organisation of invasive breast cancer driven by the interplay of active and passive nematic dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2412.01285v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In invasive breast cancer, cell clusters of varying sizes and shapes are embedded in the fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM). Although the prevailing view attributes this structure to increasing disorder resulting from loss of function and dedifferentiation, our findings reveal that it arises through a process of active self-organization driven by cancer cell motility. Simulations and histological analyses of tumours from over 2,000 breast cancer patients reveal that motile, aligned cancer cells within clusters move as active nematic aggregates through the surrounding highly aligned ECM fibres, which form a confining, passive nematic phase. Cellular motion leads to cluster splitting and coalescence. The degree of cluster activity, combined with heterogeneity in cell motility, is reflected in specific scaling behaviours for cluster shape, size distribution, and the distance between cluster boundaries and nematic defects in ECM alignment. Increased activity estimates correlate with tumour progression and are associated with a poorer prognosis for patients.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Gottheil, Saraswat Bhattacharyya, Philip Friedrich, Kilian Roth, Mario Merkel, Kolya Lettl, Kudor Harb, Salvador Rivera-Moreno, Assal Daneshgar, Jonas Wieland, Bahriye Aktas, Jens-Uwe Blohmer, Hans Kubitschke, Anne-Sophie Wegscheider, Christine Sers, Igor M. item.title: Nonequilibrium protein complexes as molecular automata
item.description: arXiv:2508.15603v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Biology stores information and computes at the molecular scale, yet the ways in which it does so are often distinct from human-engineered computers. Mapping biological computation onto architectures familiar to computer science remains an outstanding challenge. Here, inspired by Crick's proposal for molecular memory, we analyse a thermodynamically-consistent model of a protein complex subject to driven, nonequilibrium enzymatic reactions. In the strongly driven limit, we find that the system maps onto a stochastic, asynchronous variant of cellular automata, where each rule corresponds to a different set of enzymes being present. We find a broad class of phenomena in these 'molecular automata' that can be exploited for molecular computation, including error-tolerant memory via multistable attractors, and long transients that can be used as molecular stopwatches. By systematically enumerating all possible dynamical rules, we identify those that allow molecular automata to implement simple computational architectures such as finite-state machines. Overall, our results provide a framework for engineering synthetic molecular automata, and offer a route to building protein-based computation in living cells.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kocka, Kabir Husain, Jaime Agudo-Canalejo

item.title: A Polarization Hall Effect in Hydrated DNA
item.description: arXiv:2601.06089v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report magnetic-field- and temperature-dependent transverse-voltage phenomena in hydrated genomic DNA. The sample is confined beneath a glass coverslip in a quasi-two-dimensional geometry and subjected to perpendicular magnetic fields, revealing sharp thresholds, staircase-like voltage plateaus, and oscillatory structures approximately periodic in inverse magnetic field. Fixed-field cooling reveals longitudinal reorganizations near 20.6 and 12.0 $^\circ$C, while a separate experiment shows large-amplitude transverse oscillations below approximately 12 $^\circ$C. Water controls and buffer-free DNA measurements support an association between the structured response and the hydrated DNA system. We propose a polarization-based interpretation of the transverse response, termed a ``polarization Hall effect,'' and discuss the observed regimes within a phenomenological framework of nonlinear dynamics and metastable configurations. These findings identify hydrated DNA as a soft-matter system exhibiting structured electrical responses jointly regulated by magnetic field and temperature.
item.dc:creator: Mariusz Pietruszka

item.title: Uniaxial poroelastic tendon model with crimped fibre recruitment reveals hysteresis
item.description: arXiv:2606.24393v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fibre recruitment plays an important role in tendon. Due to their large water content, a popular modelling approach for tendons is poroelasticity. Within this framework some tendon studies have included fibres, though none have included crimped fibre recruitment. We present a one dimensional poroelastic model in which the solid skeleton is composed of a soft neo-Hookean background matrix and crimped fibrils which do not bear load (FIB model). As the tissue is stretched, fibrils are straightened and contribute to load bearing. The fibre-reinforced tissue is compared to a tissue with a purely neo-Hookean (NH) skeleton in response to a uniaxial constant applied load (loading) and release of the load (unloading). The system dynamics are governed by a diffusion equation where the diffusion coefficient depends on stiffness. Within tendon parameter ranges, the FIB model is softer than the NH model, and so approaches steady state more slowly during loading. The presence of stiff, crimped fibrils increases bulk extension without excessively straining the fibrils, providing a natural protection mechanism for the tendon's structural components to load, in agreement with experiments. During unloading, the FIB model is much slower to relax as the tissue softens due to fibril re-crimping. This asymmetry in loading and unloading manifests as a hysteresis loop in the stress-strain curve averaged over the tendon. The hysteresis is reduced with increasing applied load. To the authors' knowledge, the finding of hysteresis within this framework is novel. The inclusion of fibrils allows for clearer biological interpretation and potential comparison to data. While the stress law employed in this study is bespoke for the application at hand by accounting for crimp and fibril recruitment, other fibril constitutive laws can readily be considered and incorporated into this framework.
item.dc:creator: Zoe C. Godard, Sarah L. Waters, Derek E. Moulton

item.title: Towards Accurate Prediction of Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein Structure
item.description: arXiv:2609.24842v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proteins can possess numerous mutations relative to their wild-type amino acid sequences with minimal impact to their structure and function. However, in other cases, even a single amino acid mutation relative to the wild-type sequence can lead to a large change in structure or even a disease phenotype. While the accuracy of wild-type protein structure prediction has improved significantly in recent years, it remains difficult to accurately predict the structure of mutant proteins. Here, we characterize the local mutation-induced structural changes in proteins for a dataset of wildtype and the corresponding single-amino acid mutant x-ray crystal structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We find that mutation-induced structural changes in these proteins are localized at the site of the mutation, decaying rapidly with increasing spatial distance from the mutation site. In addition, we evaluate how well AlphaFold3 can recapitulate the observed mutation-induced structural deformations in the x-ray crystal structures. We find that the accuracy of the AlphaFold3 predictions decreases strongly with increasing mutation-induced deformation. In contrast to the results for AlphaFold3, the Pearson correlation between a single physical feature, i.e. the change in solvent accessibility, and the mutation-induced deformation does not depend on the magnitude of the deformation. Our results and analyses provide a framework for further studies aimed at predicting the structural changes in proteins caused by single amino acid mutations.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyi Liu, Alex Calabrese, Corey S. O'Hern

item.title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation For a Multi-Phase Alternating Renewal Random Walk
item.description: arXiv:2606.16339v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations (TURs) impose universal bounds linking current precision to entropy production in nonequilibrium systems. While general bounds like the Proesmans--Van den Broeck (PV) relation provide a broad framework, they often remain loose for processes characterized by renewal events. In this work, we derive a generalized entropic bound for current fluctuations in renewal-reward processes. By utilizing a rigorous variance decomposition within the framework of renewal-reward theory, we obtain a model-independent bound that is rigorous and, for a range of parameters in the examples considered, tighter than the PV relation evaluated with the total entropy production of the extended (position and heading) state space. Notably, in the linear-response regime, our bound correctly scales with the renewal rate and identifies a precision penalty arising from fluctuations of the cycle reward. These results provide a physically informative constraint on the precision of run-and-tumble-type dynamics and highlight the universal limits of transport in complex stochastic walkers.
item.dc:creator: Fatemeh Karimi, Farhad H. Jafarpour

item.title: The Sustainability Paradox of Biodegradable Packaging Through a Life Cycle Perspective on Chitosan Based Food Packaging
item.description: arXiv:2606.20654v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chitosan-based packaging systems are being studied as alternatives to traditional food packaging made from petroleum sources. The research that has been carried out so far has mostly focused on analyzing their material properties, formulation strategies, or biodegradable behavior. However, as a result, there is a gap left in understanding how the upstream impacts affect the functional advantages of food packaging and the end-of-life results of the formulation process. This review evaluates what trade-offs exist as well as what factors affect the sustainability of chitosan-based packages. Beginning with chitin extraction from crustacean waste, key processing steps, including demineralization, deproteinization, and nanoparticle synthesis, are assessed in terms of chemical intensity, energy demand, and associated emissions. Manufacturing routes, including solvent-based and green synthesis approaches, are compared with those of conventional plastics to identify relative environmental burdens. The use phase is analyzed with respect to antimicrobial functionality, shelf life extension, and potential reductions in food waste. End-of-life pathways, including biodegradation and composting, are evaluated alongside uncertainties related to degradation behavior and nanoparticle fate. The review takes into account life-cycle issues and offers a scientifically based viewpoint on how to differentiate between packaging applications whose environmental benefits can be determined and those whose ecological footprint, lack of functionality, and uncertainty regarding disposal make it impossible to assess sustainability.
item.dc:creator: Maria Cosic, Milena Cosic, Amy Kim, Siddhartha Pahari, Grace Wu, Rayna Zhou, Trisha Daftari, Shaily Gupta, Reyna Michelle Suneel, Srinivasan Latha, Rashi Sharma, Utkarsh Chadha

item.title: Nutrient limitation drives Turing instabilities in cross-feeding microbial communities
item.description: arXiv:2611.27534v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by metabolic interactions, often in the form of cross-feeding in which microbes exchange metabolites via diffusion through the environment. We show here that the diffusion of cross-fed metabolites generically leads to a Turing instability in resource-poor environments, driven by the feedback between local metabolite availability and cell growth. A coarse-grained model of community biomass identifies the few dimensionless parameters that control the instability, most notably the ratio of environmental energy supply to cellular maintenance costs. We find that the detailed topology of the metabolic interaction network can be coarse-grained into a single effective parameter to quantitatively characterise the instability. Beyond the onset of the instability, the community forms compact aggregates whose merger is prevented by a competition for shared resources. Overall, our results demonstrate how spatial structure can arise as an inevitable consequence of metabolic interactions in a microbial community.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kocka, Steven A. Redford, Jaime Agudo-Canalejo, Kabir Husain
